monitored_text: Resources / Materials / Natural Rubber: Properties, Examples and Uses Natural Rubber: Properties, Examples and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 35 min read Published November 25, 2026 Natural rubber is an elastic, biodegradable material derived from the latex sap of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, known as the rubber tree, and is composed primarily of cis-1,4-polyisoprene, a naturally occurring polymer. Natural rubber forms through the collection and processing of latex, a milky white fluid that flows from incisions made in the bark of rubber trees, and the material is then coagulated, dried, and refined into usable sheets or blocks. Natural rubber originates from tropical regions, with Southeast Asia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Malaysia accounting for over 90% of global production. The material exhibits a distinct set of properties, including high tensile strength ranging from 15 MPa to 30 MPa, excellent elasticity with elongation at break reaching up to 800%, and strong resistance to abrasion, tear, and fatigue. The uses of natural rubber span a wide range of industries, from automotive tire manufacturing, which consumes 70% of the world's natural rubber supply, to medical gloves, industrial conveyor belts, adhesives, footwear soles, and vibration dampers. Xometry provides access to rubber-based materials and manufacturing services suited for the precise application requirements of modern engineering and production. What Is Natural Rubber? Natural rubber is a naturally occurring elastic polymer derived from the latex of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, composed of repeating isoprene (C₅H₈) monomer units arranged in a cis-1,4 polyisoprene configuration. The polymer chain consists of 5,000 to 20,000 isoprene units covalently bonded, yielding molecular weights from 100,000 to over 1,000,000 g/mol. Its cis configuration prevents crystalline packing, which is the structural basis for its exceptional flexibility and elasticity. Harvested through tapping the bark of Hevea brasiliensis trees, fresh latex contains 30–40% rubber hydrocarbon alongside water, proteins, and mineral salts. With a glass transition temperature of -70°C, natural rubber remains flexible across most ambient conditions. Vulcanization, cross-linking polymer chains with sulfur at 140-180°C, improves tensile strength and durability while preserving elasticity, making natural rubber indispensable in high-performance applications such as aircraft tires, surgical gloves, and industrial seals. What is Natural Rubber Made Of? Natural rubber is made of polyisoprene, a long-chain polymer composed of repeating isoprene (C₅H₈) monomer units covalently bonded in a cis-1,4 configuration. Each polymer chain contains 5,000 to 20,000 isoprene units, yielding molecular weights from 100,000 to over 1,000,000 g/mol. The cis arrangement prevents tight molecular packing, which is the structural basis for its exceptional elasticity and flexibility. In its raw latex form, natural rubber also contains water, proteins, resins, sugars, and mineral salts alongside the rubber hydrocarbon. The polymer undergoes vulcanization, cross-linking with sulfur at 140-180°C, enhancing tensile strength and durability while preserving elasticity, once isolated. Where Does Natural Rubber Come From? Natural rubber comes from the Hevea brasiliensis tree, a species native to the Amazon Basin of South America, the region encompassing present-day Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia. Commercial cultivation, known as rubber plantation farming, has shifted predominantly to Southeast Asia, with Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, and India collectively producing over 90% of the global natural rubber supply. Thailand alone accounts for 35% of world production, generating around 4.5 million metric tons annually. Rubber trees thrive in tropical climates with temperatures from 25°C to 35°C, annual rainfall from 2,000 mm to 4,500 mm, and altitudes below 600 meters. A mature rubber tree, reaching harvestable age at 5 to 7 years, produces latex by tapping, a process of making shallow incisions in the bark. Each tree yields an average of 3 kg to 5 kg of dry rubber per year under standard tapping cycles. Smaller quantities of natural rubber are also sourced from alternative plants (guayule and dandelion), which are viable options for temperate-climate rubber cultivation. Is Natural Rubber a Polymer? Yes, natural rubber is a polymer. The material is a naturally occurring homopolymer of isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene), where thousands of isoprene monomer units are covalently bonded in a repeating cis-1,4 configuration to form long, flexible macromolecular chains. The degree of polymerization in natural rubber ranges from 5,000 to 20,000 isoprene units per chain, producing molecular weights from 100,000 g/mol to more than 1,000,000 g/mol. A polymer is a large molecule made of repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds. Natural rubber is a polymer whose cis-1,4 chain structure prevents tight packing, giving it high elasticity. It remains flexible at room temperature due to a low glass transition temperature (about -70°C). Vulcanization with sulfur forms cross-links between chains, increasing strength and durability while maintaining elasticity, confirming the polymer-based nature of natural rubber based on the polymer definition . How Is Natural Rubber Made? Natural rubber is made through a multi-stage process that begins with tapping the Hevea brasiliensis tree and ends with the production of dried, graded rubber sheets or technically specified rubber grades ready for industrial use. Tapping workers make a precise, diagonal cut approximately 1.5 mm deep into the bark of the rubber tree, at an angle of roughly 30 degrees, to allow latex to flow into collection cups without damaging the cambium layer beneath. The collected latex, containing 30% to 40% dry rubber content, is then transported to processing stations. A coagulating agent, formic acid at a concentration of 1% to 2%, is added to the latex to separate rubber solids from liquid serum. The coagulated rubber mass is then passed through a series of rollers to form sheets, which are either air-dried or smoke-dried in curing houses at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C over a period of 3 to 5 days. The resulting ribbed smoked sheets (RSS) or air-dried sheets are graded under international standards (ISO 2000) and compressed into bales for export. Technically specified grades (TSR or SMR) undergo additional milling, crumbling, and drying for precise industrial applications. How Is Rubber Collected From Rubber Trees? Rubber is collected from rubber trees through a manual process called tapping, which involves making precise incisions into the bark to stimulate and collect latex flow. A trained tapper uses a specialized tapping knife to cut a thin, diagonal groove typically 25 cm to 30 cm in length at a downward angle of 30 degrees on the lower half of the trunk. The cut penetrates to a depth of 1 mm to 1.5 mm, reaching just short of the cambium tissue to avoid permanent damage to the tree. Latex flows from the wound by hydrostatic pressure and is collected in a small metal or plastic cup attached below the cut. Flow continues for approximately 2 to 3 hours after tapping, yielding 30 mL to 60 mL of latex per tree per session. Tapping takes place in the early morning hours, typically from 5:00 AM to 7:00 AM, when internal tree pressure is highest. A tree is tapped on alternating days or every third day, depending on the tapping system applied, with the tapping panel renewed by removing a thin slice with each cut, allowing the tree a productive life of 25 to 30 years. Is Natural Rubber Extracted From Latex? Yes, natural rubber is extracted from latex. Latex is the milky, colloidal suspension found in the latex vessels of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, and it serves as the direct raw material from which natural rubber is isolated. Fresh latex contains 30% to 40% rubber hydrocarbon, 55% to 65% water, and small amounts of proteins, resins, sugars, and mineral salts. The rubber particles within latex are spherical, negatively charged, and range from 0.02 µm to 3 µm in diameter. Extraction from latex is achieved through coagulation, centrifugation, or evaporation, depending on the intended product form. Coagulation using formic or acetic acid destabilizes the latex colloid and causes rubber particles to aggregate, forming a solid mass that is then processed into sheets or technically specified grades. Centrifugation concentrates latex to 60% or higher dry rubber content, producing concentrated latex used directly in dip-molded products (gloves and condoms). Thermoplastic rubber (TPR), a synthetic alternative, is not derived from latex but is produced through synthetic petrochemical processes, highlighting the distinction between TPR vs. Latex . What Are the Properties of Natural Rubber? The properties of natural rubber are listed below. High Tensile Strength: Natural rubber has a tensile strength ranging from 15 MPa to 30 MPa in its vulcanized form, making it capable of withstanding considerable pulling forces without rupturing. The long polymer chains and cross-link density achieved through vulcanization are the primary contributors to the tensile performance of natural rubber. Exceptional Elasticity: The elongation at break of natural rubber reaches up to 800% in optimized vulcanized compounds, allowing the material to stretch significantly and return to its original shape without permanent deformation. The cis-1,4-polyisoprene chain configuration provides the molecular flexibility responsible for the elasticity. Low Hysteresis: Natural rubber exhibits low heat buildup under repeated deformation cycles, a property quantified by a low hysteresis loss value, making it preferred in tire applications where heat generation affects durability and rolling resistance. Good Tear Resistance: The tear strength of natural rubber compounds ranges from 30 kN/m to 100 kN/m, depending on compounding and vulcanization conditions, providing resistance to propagation of cuts and nicks under mechanical stress. Temperature Sensitivity: Natural rubber performs well at temperatures from −50°C to 80°C, but begins to soften and lose mechanical integrity above 80°C. Prolonged exposure to temperatures above 100°C causes oxidative degradation. Limited Chemical Resistance: Natural rubber resists water and dilute aqueous solutions but degrades rapidly when exposed to petroleum-based oils, ozone, strong oxidizing agents, and aromatic solvents. What Physical Properties Does Natural Rubber Have? The physical properties of natural rubber determine its elasticity, flexibility, hardness, thermal behavior, and frictional performance under different operating conditions. Natural rubber has a density ranging from 0.91 g/cm³ to 0.93 g/cm³ in its raw state, making it a lightweight elastic material used in engineering and industrial products. The hardness of vulcanized natural rubber compounds ranges from 30 Shore A to 90 Shore A, depending on sulfur content and formulation additives used during vulcanization. The glass transition temperature (Tg) of natural rubber is −70°C, allowing the material to remain flexible at low temperatures. The elastic modulus of natural rubber ranges from 0.01 GPa to 0.1 GPa, which supports large elastic deformation under relatively low stress. Natural rubber also has low thermal conductivity, 0.13 W/m·K to 0.16 W/m·K, classifying it as a thermal insulator. Its coefficient of friction ranges from 1.0 to 4.0 on dry surfaces, supporting non-slip and traction-based applications. What Mechanical Properties Does Natural Rubber Have? The mechanical properties of natural rubber determine its elasticity, strength, flexibility, and resistance to repeated deformation under mechanical loading. Natural rubber has high tensile strength, typically ranging from 20 MPa to 30 MPa, along with elongation at break values between 500% and 700%. The material also exhibits excellent elasticity and resilience, allowing it to return to its original shape after stretching or compression. Natural rubber possesses good tear strength, abrasion resistance, and fatigue resistance under cyclic loading conditions. These mechanical properties support its use in tires, seals, vibration isolators, and flexible industrial components. Is Natural Rubber Flexible and Elastic? Yes, natural rubber is flexible and elastic. The flexibility and elasticity of natural rubber originate from the molecular architecture of cis-1,4-polyisoprene, where the cis double bond at every isoprene unit creates a kinked, coiled chain conformation that allows extensive reversible deformation under mechanical stress. The elongation at break of vulcanized natural rubber reaches up to 800%, and the material recovers its original dimensions with negligible permanent set when deformation falls within the elastic limit. The elastic modulus of natural rubber ranges from 0.01 GPa to 0.1 GPa, which is substantially lower than most metals and rigid plastics, confirming the material's capacity to deform under minimal applied force. Flexibility is maintained at temperatures as low as −50°C due to the low glass transition temperature (Tg) of approximately −70°C, ensuring the material does not become brittle in cold environments. The combination of high elasticity and low hysteresis loss, meaning minimal heat generation per deformation cycle, makes natural rubber a preferred material in dynamic applications (tires, engine mounts, and seismic isolators), where repeated deformation is a primary service condition. How Does Polymer Relate to Natural Rubber? Polymer relates to natural rubber as the fundamental structural classification that defines the material's composition and behavior. Natural rubber is a polymer, a high-molecular-weight homopolymer of isoprene, where the repeating monomer unit is cis-1,4-isoprene (C₅H₈). The degree of polymerization, referring to the number of isoprene units per chain, ranges from 5,000 to 20,000 units, producing molecular weights from 100,000 g/mol to over 1,000,000 g/mol. The polymer nature of natural rubber is directly responsible for its mechanical properties. Long, entangled polymer chains provide the material's high tensile strength and resistance to deformation. The cis stereochemistry prevents crystallization at rest but causes strain-crystallization during stretching, increasing molecular reinforcement and enabling tensile strengths up to 30 MPa in unfilled natural rubber. Cross-linking the polymer chains through vulcanization forms a three-dimensional network, transforming the material from a thermoplastic-like soft solid to a thermoset elastomer with defined mechanical characteristics suited to engineering applications. Xometry supplies rubber polymer materials and rubber-based components for manufacturing projects requiring precise mechanical and chemical specifications. Why Is Natural Rubber Classified as a Polymer Material? Natural rubber is classified as a polymer material because it is entirely composed of macromolecular chains formed by the covalent bonding of repeating isoprene monomer units (C₅H₈) in a cis-1,4 configuration. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) definition of a polymer requires a substance to consist of molecules characterized by the multiple repetition of one or more species of atoms or groups of atoms, which natural rubber fully satisfies through its polyisoprene chain structure. The classification as a polymer material is further confirmed by the molecular weight range of natural rubber chains, spanning from 100,000 g/mol to more than 1,000,000 g/mol, which is characteristic of high-polymer behavior. The material exhibits all the defining behaviors of polymer materials, including viscoelasticity, a glass transition temperature (Tg) of −70°C, and the ability to undergo cross-linking reactions. Strain-induced crystallization, a molecular phenomenon unique to polymer materials with regular chain architecture, occurs in natural rubber when stretched beyond 300% elongation, further reinforcing its classification as a semi-crystallizable polymer under mechanical deformation. Is Natural Rubber a Naturally Occurring Polymer? Yes, natural rubber is a naturally occurring polymer, produced biosynthetically within the latex vessels of the Hevea brasiliensis tree through enzymatic polymerization of isoprene precursors. The following characteristics confirm the naturally occurring polymer classification of natural rubber are listed below. Biosynthetic Origin: The polymerization of isoprene units in natural rubber occurs through the action of the enzyme cis-prenyltransferase within living plant cells, producing chains with consistent cis-1,4 stereochemistry without any industrial chemical intervention. The biological precision of the enzymatic process yields molecular weights exceeding 1,000,000 g/mol. Regular Stereochemistry: The cis-1,4 configuration of each isoprene unit along the natural rubber chain is a direct product of biological synthesis, distinguishing natural rubber from synthetic trans-1,4-polyisoprene (gutta-percha), which has different mechanical properties despite sharing the same chemical formula. Biodegradability: Natural rubber degrades through microbial activity by bacteria (Nocardia and Gordonia species) that produce rubber oxygenase enzymes capable of cleaving polyisoprene chains. Degradation rates are affected by environmental conditions, including temperature, moisture, and UV exposure. Non-petroleum Origin: Natural rubber is derived entirely from biological carbon fixed through photosynthesis, requiring no petroleum feedstocks, which distinguishes it from synthetic polymers produced through petrochemical polymerization. What Are Synthetic Polymers in Relation to Synthetic Rubber? Synthetic polymers, in relation to synthetic rubber, are the artificially produced macromolecular materials from which all synthetic rubber types are manufactured through petrochemical polymerization processes. Synthetic rubbers are a specific subclass of synthetic polymers engineered to replicate or exceed specific properties of natural rubber by selecting different monomer units and polymerization methods. Common synthetic rubber types (styrene-butadiene rubber [SBR], nitrile rubber [NBR], neoprene [CR], and ethylene propylene diene monomer rubber [EPDM] ) are all synthetic polymers produced from petroleum-derived monomers. The global production of synthetic rubber reached 15 million metric tons in 2023, compared to approximately 14 million metric tons of natural rubber, reflecting the broad industrial adoption of synthetic polymer-based elastomers. Synthetic polymers used in rubber production are classified by their backbone chemistry, carbon-chain polymers (SBR, NBR) and heterochain polymers (silicone rubber), with each class offering a distinct performance profile. Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) is a copolymer of styrene and butadiene and the most widely used synthetic rubber. It provides high abrasion resistance and is commonly used in tire manufacturing, showing the importance of Synthetic Polymers . How Is Synthetic Rubber Classified as a Synthetic Polymer? Synthetic rubber is classified as a synthetic polymer because its macromolecular chains are produced entirely through industrial polymerization of petrochemical monomers, with no biological or natural source of the repeating units. The American Chemical Society (ACS) and IUPAC classify any polymer as synthetic when the polymerization reaction is initiated and controlled through industrial processes (free radical, anionic, cationic, or coordination polymerization) rather than biological enzymatic activity. Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), the largest-volume synthetic rubber, is produced by the emulsion or solution polymerization of styrene and 1,3-butadiene at temperatures from 5°C to 50°C, depending on the polymerization process. Nitrile rubber (NBR) is classified as a synthetic polymer through the copolymerization of acrylonitrile (18% to 50%) and butadiene, giving the material its characteristic oil resistance. Neoprene (polychloroprene) is synthesized from chloroprene monomers through free-radical emulsion polymerization at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C. The designation "synthetic" further distinguishes these materials from natural rubber in regulatory, material specification, and supply chain documentation across industries using ASTM and ISO rubber classification standards. Is Synthetic Rubber a Man Made Polymer Material? Yes, synthetic rubber is a man-made polymer material. Each synthetic rubber type is produced through deliberate industrial polymerization of monomers derived from petroleum refining and petrochemical processing, with no component of the final polymer originating from a biological or natural source. The classification as man-made is confirmed by the entire synthesis chain: petroleum is cracked to produce monomer feedstocks (butadiene, styrene, isoprene, acrylonitrile), which are then polymerized in controlled industrial reactors using chemical initiators, catalysts, and process conditions set by engineers. The first commercially produced man-made synthetic rubber, Buna-S (a styrene-butadiene copolymer), was developed in Germany in the 1930s, establishing the foundation for the synthetic polymer rubber industry. Modern synthetic rubber production relies on Ziegler-Natta and metallocene catalysts to achieve precise control of polymer stereochemistry, molecular weight, and chain distribution, parameters that are impossible to engineer in naturally occurring rubber. The man-made nature of synthetic rubber enables consistent batch-to-batch chemical composition, a quality control advantage not achievable with natural rubber derived from agricultural harvesting. How Do Thermoplastic Elastomers Compare to Natural Rubber? Thermoplastic elastomers (TPEs) are compared to natural rubber across multiple material performance and processing dimensions. Natural rubber provides superior elongation at break, compression set resistance, and strain-induced crystallization, while Thermoplastic Elastomers offer easier recyclability and efficient thermoplastic melt-processing capabilities. Thermoplastic elastomers compared to natural rubber are shown in the table below. What Ways do TPE Materials Differ From Natural Rubber? TPE materials differ from natural rubber across processing, performance, structural, and environmental dimensions. TPE materials differ from natural rubber are listed below. Processing Mechanism: TPE materials are processed using conventional thermoplastic equipment (injection molding machines and extruders) at melt temperatures from 180°C to 260°C, and the material solidifies upon cooling without any chemical cross-linking reaction. Natural rubber requires vulcanization, a chemical cross-linking process using sulfur at 140°C to 180°C, which permanently sets the material's network structure. Molecular Structure: TPE materials consist of physically cross-linked block copolymer chains (hard-block and soft-block segments) that dissociate upon heating, allowing reprocessing. Natural rubber chains are covalently cross-linked during vulcanization, forming a permanent three-dimensional network that cannot be remelted. Recyclability: The physically cross-linked structure of TPEs allows the material to be remelted and reprocessed multiple times with minimal property degradation, reducing material waste. Vulcanized natural rubber cannot be remelted due to permanent covalent cross-links. Compression Set: Natural rubber exhibits a compression set of less than 20% under standard ASTM D395 conditions, while TPE materials show compression set values from 20% to 50%, indicating greater permanent deformation under sustained compressive loads. Chemical Resistance: Thermoplastic elastomers (TPE-V and TPE-E types) offer moderate resistance to oils and fuels, while natural rubber degrades rapidly on contact with petroleum-based oils and aromatic solvents Can Thermoplastic Elastomers be Recycled Like Plastics? Yes, Thermoplastic elastomers (TPEs) can be recycled like plastics because they soften when heated and can be remelted, reshaped, and reprocessed multiple times. TPEs contain reversible physical crosslinks that separate during heating and reform during cooling, unlike vulcanized natural rubber, which contains permanent crosslinked networks that prevent remelting. The structure allows mechanical recycling through grinding, melting, extrusion, and pelletizing processes commonly used for plastics. Thermoplastic elastomers combine the elastic behavior of rubber with the reprocessability of plastics, where plastics are polymer-based materials that can be molded or reshaped through heat and pressure during manufacturing, which relates to the Plastic Definition . How Does Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) Differ From Natural Rubber Latex? Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) differs from natural rubber latex mainly in structure and processing. Natural rubber latex is a natural polymer (polyisoprene) that is chemically vulcanized, forming permanent crosslinks. Natural rubber latex is a natural polymer (polyisoprene) that is chemically vulcanized, forming permanent crosslinks. It cannot be melted or remolded once cured, but it offers very high elasticity, tensile strength, and fatigue resistance. Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) is a synthetic thermoplastic elastomer with reversible physical crosslinks, allowing it to soften when heated, be remolded, and recycled like plastic. It is easier and cheaper to process, but generally has lower mechanical performance than natural rubber. Natural rubber is non-recyclable after curing and stronger, while TPR is recyclable, easier to process, and more manufacturing-friendly, referred to as Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR). What Are the Main Differences Between TPR and Latex in Performance? The main differences between TPR and Latex in Performance are listed below. Tensile Strength: Natural rubber latex compounds achieve tensile strengths from 15 MPa to 30 MPa due to strain-induced crystallization of the cis-polyisoprene chains. TPR compounds (SBS-based) typically range from 10 MPa to 25 MPa, with strength dependent on the styrene content and block copolymer architecture. Elongation at Break: Latex-based natural rubber reaches elongation at break values of 500% to 800%, while TPR materials generally achieve 300% to 600%, depending on grade and formulation. Compression Set: Vulcanized latex exhibits compression set values below 20% (ASTM D395), indicating excellent recovery from sustained compression. TPR compounds show compression set values from 20% to 50%, reflecting greater permanent deformation under prolonged compressive loading. Heat Resistance: Natural rubber latex products begin to soften and degrade above 80°C with continuous exposure. TPR materials retain structural integrity up to 100°C to 120°C, depending on the hard-block composition. Chemical Resistance: Natural rubber latex degrades rapidly with petroleum-based oils, aromatic solvents, and strong oxidizers. TPR materials, particularly SBS grades, offer better resistance to aliphatic oils and dilute chemical environments. Allergen Profile: Natural rubber latex contains Hev b proteins that cause Type I latex hypersensitivity in 1% to 6% of the population. TPR contains no natural proteins and presents no latex allergen risk. Is TPR Considered a Thermoplastic Elastomer? Yes, TPR is considered a thermoplastic elastomer. Thermoplastic rubber (TPR) satisfies the definition of a thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) by combining the processing characteristics of thermoplastics, the ability to melt and be reprocessed, with the elastic, rubber-like behavior of elastomers at ambient service temperatures. TPR is classified within the TPE-S (styrenic block copolymer) subclass of thermoplastic elastomers under ISO 18064, which includes SBS (styrene-butadiene-styrene) and SIS (styrene-isoprene-styrene) block copolymers. The hard polystyrene blocks in TPR act as physical cross-link domains, providing dimensional stability and strength, while the soft rubber midblock (polybutadiene or polyisoprene) provides elasticity and flexibility. The hardness of TPR grades ranges from 20 Shore A to 60 Shore A, placing the material firmly within the elastomer classification alongside vulcanized rubber compounds. How Is Silicone Different From Natural Rubber? Silicone differs from natural rubber mainly in its chemical structure, temperature stability, and durability. Natural rubber is an organic polymer (polyisoprene) derived from latex and strengthened through vulcanization, giving it high elasticity and good mechanical strength but limited resistance to heat, ozone, and aging. Silicone is a synthetic elastomer made from silicon–oxygen (Si–O) backbone chains, which gives it exceptional thermal stability, chemical inertness, and resistance to weathering, UV radiation, and extreme temperatures. Natural rubber generally provides better tensile strength and tear resistance, while silicone offers superior flexibility over a wide temperature range (from very low to high heat), better electrical insulation, and longer environmental durability. Silicone is less resistant to abrasion and has lower mechanical strength compared to natural rubber. Natural rubber is preferred for high-strength mechanical applications, while silicone is chosen for environments requiring heat resistance, stability, and long-term durability, which is why it is widely used in Silicone Uses . What Property Differences Exist Between Silicone and Latex? The property differences between Silicone and Latex are listed below. Temperature Range: Silicone maintains mechanical integrity from -60°C to 230°C, making it suitable for high-temperature and cryogenic applications. Natural rubber latex performs reliably from -50°C to 80°C, restricting its use in extreme thermal environments. Tensile Strength: Natural rubber latex achieves tensile strengths from 15 MPa to 30 MPa, significantly higher than silicone's typical range of 3 MPa to 10 MPa. The superior tensile strength of latex makes it preferred for thin-walled elastic products (gloves and condoms) where high elongation and tear resistance are required. Ozone Resistance: Silicone exhibits excellent ozone resistance across all service conditions. Natural rubber latex begins to crack at ozone concentrations as low as 0.01 ppm, requiring antiozonant additives in outdoor applications. Chemical Resistance: Silicone resists dilute acids, alkalis, water, and many polar solvents but degrades with aliphatic hydrocarbons and concentrated solvents. Natural rubber latex degrades rapidly with petroleum-based oils, aromatic solvents, and strong oxidizing agents. Biocompatibility: Medical-grade silicone is fully biocompatible with human tissue and is approved for long-term implantation by the FDA. Natural rubber latex contains Hev b proteins, causing Type I hypersensitivity reactions in 1% to 6% of the general population, limiting use in medical-grade applications. Is Silicone More Heat Resistant Than Natural Rubber? Yes, silicone is more heat-resistant than natural rubber. The superior heat resistance of silicone originates from the silicon-oxygen (Si-O) backbone of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), the base polymer of silicone rubber, which has a bond dissociation energy of approximately 452 kJ/mol, significantly higher than the C-C bond energy of 346 kJ/mol in natural rubber's polyisoprene chain. Silicone retains its elastic properties and structural integrity at continuous service temperatures up to 230°C, with some specialty silicone grades rated for intermittent exposure up to 300°C. Natural rubber begins to soften and undergo oxidative degradation at temperatures above 80°C under continuous service, and accelerated deterioration, including chain scission and hardening, occurs above 120°C. At 200°C, natural rubber undergoes rapid thermal decomposition, producing volatile degradation products that eliminate the material's functional properties. In standardized heat aging tests (ASTM D573), silicone compounds retain over 80% of their original tensile strength after 70 hours at 200°C, while natural rubber compounds show severe degradation under identical conditions, confirming silicone's substantial thermal performance advantage over natural rubber. What Are Common Examples of Natural Rubber Products? The common examples of natural rubber products are listed below. Pneumatic Tires: Natural rubber constitutes 40% to 45% of the rubber compound in passenger car tires and up to 80% in truck and aircraft tires, where high tensile strength and low heat buildup are critical performance requirements. The strain-induced crystallization of natural rubber under dynamic loading conditions makes it irreplaceable in high-performance tire construction. Surgical and Examination Gloves: Latex surgical gloves are manufactured from concentrated natural rubber latex (60% dry rubber content) through dip-coating processes, producing thin films with wall thicknesses of 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm that combine barrier protection with tactile sensitivity. Latex Condoms: Natural rubber latex condoms have a tensile strength exceeding 18 MPa and elongation at break above 700%, with wall thicknesses of 0.05 mm to 0.08 mm, meeting ISO 4074 standards for mechanical integrity and viral barrier performance. Industrial Conveyor Belts: Natural rubber is the primary cover and carcass material in heavy-duty conveyor belts used in mining and quarrying, where tensile strengths of 20 MPa to 28 MPa and high abrasion resistance are service requirements. Elastic Bands: Standard rubber bands contain vulcanized natural rubber with elongation at break from 600% to 800%, maintaining elasticity over thousands of stretch-and-release cycles without permanent deformation. Which Everyday Items Are Made From Natural Rubber? Everyday items made from natural rubber are listed below. Rubber Bands: Rubber bands are manufactured from vulcanized natural rubber and are designed to stretch to 6 to 8 times their original length without breaking. The natural rubber compound provides the elastic recovery needed for secure bundling of papers, food packaging, and other applications requiring repeated use. Balloons: Latex balloons are produced by dip-coating balloon-shaped molds in natural rubber latex, with wall thicknesses of 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm. Natural rubber latex provides the high elongation at break (700%+) and gas impermeability required for balloon applications. Shoe Soles: Natural rubber soles used in athletic footwear and work boots provide abrasion resistance (low DIN 53516 abrasion loss) and a high coefficient of friction (1.5 to 3.5) on wet and dry surfaces. Natural rubber outsoles are a standard feature in high-performance sports footwear. Erasers: Standard pencil erasers use natural rubber as the base elastomer, with the soft consistency 30 Shore A to 40 Shore A hardness allowing effective abrasion of graphite particles from paper surfaces. Garden Hoses: Reinforced garden hoses use inner tubes of natural rubber for flexibility in temperatures from -10°C to 60°C and pressure ratings up to 10 bar. Are Rubber Bands Made From Natural Rubber? Yes, rubber bands are made from natural rubber. The standard rubber band is manufactured from a vulcanized natural rubber compound, where the base polyisoprene provides the high elongation at break (600% to 800%) and elastic recovery that defines the product's functional performance. The vulcanization of the rubber band compound uses sulfur at concentrations from 2 to 5 parts per hundred rubber (phr), creating a cross-linked network that enables thousands of stretch-and-release cycles without permanent deformation. The extrusion process forms the rubber compound into long, flat strips, which are then cut into bands of specified widths and circumferences. Standard rubber band dimensions follow ASTM D5181 specifications, with widths from 3 mm to 25 mm and lengths from 35 mm to 180 mm. Alliance Rubber Company, one of the largest rubber band manufacturers, reports that natural rubber is used for 95%+ of its standard product line due to the superior elastic recovery and fatigue resistance that natural rubber provides compared to synthetic alternatives. sections.heading: What Is Natural Rubber?
sections.text: What Is Natural Rubber? Natural rubber is a naturally occurring elastic polymer derived from the latex of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, composed of repeating isoprene (C₅H₈) monomer units arranged in a cis-1,4 polyisoprene configuration. The polymer chain consists of 5,000 to 20,000 isoprene units covalently bonded, yielding molecular weights from 100,000 to over 1,000,000 g/mol. Its cis configuration prevents crystalline packing, which is the structural basis for its exceptional flexibility and elasticity. Harvested through tapping the bark of Hevea brasiliensis trees, fresh latex contains 30–40% rubber hydrocarbon alongside water, proteins, and mineral salts. With a glass transition temperature of -70°C, natural rubber remains flexible across most ambient conditions. Vulcanization, cross-linking polymer chains with sulfur at 140-180°C, improves tensile strength and durability while preserving elasticity, making natural rubber indispensable in high-performance applications such as aircraft tires, surgical gloves, and industrial seals. sections.heading: Where Does Natural Rubber Come From?
sections.text: Where Does Natural Rubber Come From? Natural rubber comes from the Hevea brasiliensis tree, a species native to the Amazon Basin of South America, the region encompassing present-day Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia. Commercial cultivation, known as rubber plantation farming, has shifted predominantly to Southeast Asia, with Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, and India collectively producing over 90% of the global natural rubber supply. Thailand alone accounts for 35% of world production, generating around 4.5 million metric tons annually. Rubber trees thrive in tropical climates with temperatures from 25°C to 35°C, annual rainfall from 2,000 mm to 4,500 mm, and altitudes below 600 meters. A mature rubber tree, reaching harvestable age at 5 to 7 years, produces latex by tapping, a process of making shallow incisions in the bark. Each tree yields an average of 3 kg to 5 kg of dry rubber per year under standard tapping cycles. Smaller quantities of natural rubber are also sourced from alternative plants (guayule and dandelion), which are viable options for temperate-climate rubber cultivation. Is Natural Rubber a Polymer? sections.heading: How Is Natural Rubber Made?
sections.text: How Is Natural Rubber Made? Natural rubber is made through a multi-stage process that begins with tapping the Hevea brasiliensis tree and ends with the production of dried, graded rubber sheets or technically specified rubber grades ready for industrial use. Tapping workers make a precise, diagonal cut approximately 1.5 mm deep into the bark of the rubber tree, at an angle of roughly 30 degrees, to allow latex to flow into collection cups without damaging the cambium layer beneath. The collected latex, containing 30% to 40% dry rubber content, is then transported to processing stations. A coagulating agent, formic acid at a concentration of 1% to 2%, is added to the latex to separate rubber solids from liquid serum. The coagulated rubber mass is then passed through a series of rollers to form sheets, which are either air-dried or smoke-dried in curing houses at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C over a period of 3 to 5 days. The resulting ribbed smoked sheets (RSS) or air-dried sheets are graded under international standards (ISO 2000) and compressed into bales for export. sections.heading: How Is Rubber Collected From Rubber Trees?
sections.text: How Is Rubber Collected From Rubber Trees? Rubber is collected from rubber trees through a manual process called tapping, which involves making precise incisions into the bark to stimulate and collect latex flow. A trained tapper uses a specialized tapping knife to cut a thin, diagonal groove typically 25 cm to 30 cm in length at a downward angle of 30 degrees on the lower half of the trunk. The cut penetrates to a depth of 1 mm to 1.5 mm, reaching just short of the cambium tissue to avoid permanent damage to the tree. Latex flows from the wound by hydrostatic pressure and is collected in a small metal or plastic cup attached below the cut. Flow continues for approximately 2 to 3 hours after tapping, yielding 30 mL to 60 mL of latex per tree per session. Tapping takes place in the early morning hours, typically from 5:00 AM to 7:00 AM, when internal tree pressure is highest. A tree is tapped on alternating days or every third day, depending on the tapping system applied, with the tapping panel renewed by removing a thin slice with each cut, allowing the tree a productive life of 25 to 30 years. sections.heading: What Are the Properties of Natural Rubber?
sections.text: What Are the Properties of Natural Rubber? The properties of natural rubber are listed below. High Tensile Strength: Natural rubber has a tensile strength ranging from 15 MPa to 30 MPa in its vulcanized form, making it capable of withstanding considerable pulling forces without rupturing. The long polymer chains and cross-link density achieved through vulcanization are the primary contributors to the tensile performance of natural rubber. Exceptional Elasticity: The elongation at break of natural rubber reaches up to 800% in optimized vulcanized compounds, allowing the material to stretch significantly and return to its original shape without permanent deformation. The cis-1,4-polyisoprene chain configuration provides the molecular flexibility responsible for the elasticity. Low Hysteresis: Natural rubber exhibits low heat buildup under repeated deformation cycles, a property quantified by a low hysteresis loss value, making it preferred in tire applications where heat generation affects durability and rolling resistance. Good Tear Resistance: The tear strength of natural rubber compounds ranges from 30 kN/m to 100 kN/m, depending on compounding and vulcanization conditions, provi...

sections.heading: What Physical Properties Does Natural Rubber Have?
sections.text: What Physical Properties Does Natural Rubber Have? The physical properties of natural rubber determine its elasticity, flexibility, hardness, thermal behavior, and frictional performance under different operating conditions. Natural rubber has a density ranging from 0.91 g/cm³ to 0.93 g/cm³ in its raw state, making it a lightweight elastic material used in engineering and industrial products. The hardness of vulcanized natural rubber compounds ranges from 30 Shore A to 90 Shore A, depending on sulfur content and formulation additives used during vulcanization. The glass transition temperature (Tg) of natural rubber is −70°C, allowing the material to remain flexible at low temperatures. The elastic modulus of natural rubber ranges from 0.01 GPa to 0.1 GPa, which supports large elastic deformation under relatively low stress. Natural rubber also has low thermal conductivity, 0.13 W/m·K to 0.16 W/m·K, classifying it as a thermal insulator. Its coefficient of friction ranges from 1.0 to 4.0 on dry surfaces, supporting non-slip and traction-based applications. What Mechanical Properties Does Natural Rubber Have? sections.heading: Is Natural Rubber Flexible and Elastic?
sections.text: Is Natural Rubber Flexible and Elastic? Yes, natural rubber is flexible and elastic. The flexibility and elasticity of natural rubber originate from the molecular architecture of cis-1,4-polyisoprene, where the cis double bond at every isoprene unit creates a kinked, coiled chain conformation that allows extensive reversible deformation under mechanical stress. The elongation at break of vulcanized natural rubber reaches up to 800%, and the material recovers its original dimensions with negligible permanent set when deformation falls within the elastic limit. The elastic modulus of natural rubber ranges from 0.01 GPa to 0.1 GPa, which is substantially lower than most metals and rigid plastics, confirming the material's capacity to deform under minimal applied force. Flexibility is maintained at temperatures as low as −50°C due to the low glass transition temperature (Tg) of approximately −70°C, ensuring the material does not become brittle in cold environments. The combination of high elasticity and low hysteresis loss, meaning minimal heat generation per deformation cycle, makes natural rubber a preferred material in dynamic applications (tires, engine mounts, and seismic isolato...

sections.heading: How Does Polymer Relate to Natural Rubber?
sections.text: How Does Polymer Relate to Natural Rubber? Polymer relates to natural rubber as the fundamental structural classification that defines the material's composition and behavior. Natural rubber is a polymer, a high-molecular-weight homopolymer of isoprene, where the repeating monomer unit is cis-1,4-isoprene (C₅H₈). The degree of polymerization, referring to the number of isoprene units per chain, ranges from 5,000 to 20,000 units, producing molecular weights from 100,000 g/mol to over 1,000,000 g/mol. The polymer nature of natural rubber is directly responsible for its mechanical properties. Long, entangled polymer chains provide the material's high tensile strength and resistance to deformation. The cis stereochemistry prevents crystallization at rest but causes strain-crystallization during stretching, increasing molecular reinforcement and enabling tensile strengths up to 30 MPa in unfilled natural rubber. Cross-linking the polymer chains through vulcanization forms a three-dimensional network, transforming the material from a thermoplastic-like soft solid to a thermoset elastomer with defined mechanical characteristics suited to engineering applications. sections.heading: Why Is Natural Rubber Classified as a Polymer Material?
sections.text: Why Is Natural Rubber Classified as a Polymer Material? Natural rubber is classified as a polymer material because it is entirely composed of macromolecular chains formed by the covalent bonding of repeating isoprene monomer units (C₅H₈) in a cis-1,4 configuration. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) definition of a polymer requires a substance to consist of molecules characterized by the multiple repetition of one or more species of atoms or groups of atoms, which natural rubber fully satisfies through its polyisoprene chain structure. The classification as a polymer material is further confirmed by the molecular weight range of natural rubber chains, spanning from 100,000 g/mol to more than 1,000,000 g/mol, which is characteristic of high-polymer behavior. The material exhibits all the defining behaviors of polymer materials, including viscoelasticity, a glass transition temperature (Tg) of −70°C, and the ability to undergo cross-linking reactions. sections.heading: What Are Synthetic Polymers in Relation to Synthetic Rubber?
sections.text: What Are Synthetic Polymers in Relation to Synthetic Rubber? Synthetic polymers, in relation to synthetic rubber, are the artificially produced macromolecular materials from which all synthetic rubber types are manufactured through petrochemical polymerization processes. Synthetic rubbers are a specific subclass of synthetic polymers engineered to replicate or exceed specific properties of natural rubber by selecting different monomer units and polymerization methods. Common synthetic rubber types (styrene-butadiene rubber [SBR], nitrile rubber [NBR], neoprene [CR], and ethylene propylene diene monomer rubber [EPDM] ) are all synthetic polymers produced from petroleum-derived monomers. The global production of synthetic rubber reached 15 million metric tons in 2023, compared to approximately 14 million metric tons of natural rubber, reflecting the broad industrial adoption of synthetic polymer-based elastomers. Synthetic polymers used in rubber production are classified by their backbone chemistry, carbon-chain polymers (SBR, NBR) and heterochain polymers (silicone rubber), with each class offering a distinct performance profile. sections.heading: How Is Synthetic Rubber Classified as a Synthetic Polymer?
sections.text: How Is Synthetic Rubber Classified as a Synthetic Polymer? Synthetic rubber is classified as a synthetic polymer because its macromolecular chains are produced entirely through industrial polymerization of petrochemical monomers, with no biological or natural source of the repeating units. The American Chemical Society (ACS) and IUPAC classify any polymer as synthetic when the polymerization reaction is initiated and controlled through industrial processes (free radical, anionic, cationic, or coordination polymerization) rather than biological enzymatic activity. Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), the largest-volume synthetic rubber, is produced by the emulsion or solution polymerization of styrene and 1,3-butadiene at temperatures from 5°C to 50°C, depending on the polymerization process. Nitrile rubber (NBR) is classified as a synthetic polymer through the copolymerization of acrylonitrile (18% to 50%) and butadiene, giving the material its characteristic oil resistance. Neoprene (polychloroprene) is synthesized from chloroprene monomers through free-radical emulsion polymerization at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C. sections.heading: What Ways do TPE Materials Differ From Natural Rubber?
sections.text: What Ways do TPE Materials Differ From Natural Rubber? TPE materials differ from natural rubber across processing, performance, structural, and environmental dimensions. TPE materials differ from natural rubber are listed below. Processing Mechanism: TPE materials are processed using conventional thermoplastic equipment (injection molding machines and extruders) at melt temperatures from 180°C to 260°C, and the material solidifies upon cooling without any chemical cross-linking reaction. Natural rubber requires vulcanization, a chemical cross-linking process using sulfur at 140°C to 180°C, which permanently sets the material's network structure. Molecular Structure: TPE materials consist of physically cross-linked block copolymer chains (hard-block and soft-block segments) that dissociate upon heating, allowing reprocessing. Natural rubber chains are covalently cross-linked during vulcanization, forming a permanent three-dimensional network that cannot be remelted. sections.text: How Does Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) Differ From Natural Rubber Latex? Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) differs from natural rubber latex mainly in structure and processing. Natural rubber latex is a natural polymer (polyisoprene) that is chemically vulcanized, forming permanent crosslinks. Natural rubber latex is a natural polymer (polyisoprene) that is chemically vulcanized, forming permanent crosslinks. It cannot be melted or remolded once cured, but it offers very high elasticity, tensile strength, and fatigue resistance. Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) is a synthetic thermoplastic elastomer with reversible physical crosslinks, allowing it to soften when heated, be remolded, and recycled like plastic. It is easier and cheaper to process, but generally has lower mechanical performance than natural rubber. Natural rubber is non-recyclable after curing and stronger, while TPR is recyclable, easier to process, and more manufacturing-friendly, referred to as Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR).

sections.heading: What Are the Main Differences Between TPR and Latex in Performance?
sections.text: What Are the Main Differences Between TPR and Latex in Performance? The main differences between TPR and Latex in Performance are listed below. Tensile Strength: Natural rubber latex compounds achieve tensile strengths from 15 MPa to 30 MPa due to strain-induced crystallization of the cis-polyisoprene chains. TPR compounds (SBS-based) typically range from 10 MPa to 25 MPa, with strength dependent on the styrene content and block copolymer architecture. Elongation at Break: Latex-based natural rubber reaches elongation at break values of 500% to 800%, while TPR materials generally achieve 300% to 600%, depending on grade and formulation. Compression Set: Vulcanized latex exhibits compression set values below 20% (ASTM D395), indicating excellent recovery from sustained compression. TPR compounds show compression set values from 20% to 50%, reflecting greater permanent deformation under prolonged compressive loading. sections.heading: How Is Silicone Different From Natural Rubber?
sections.text: How Is Silicone Different From Natural Rubber? Silicone differs from natural rubber mainly in its chemical structure, temperature stability, and durability. Natural rubber is an organic polymer (polyisoprene) derived from latex and strengthened through vulcanization, giving it high elasticity and good mechanical strength but limited resistance to heat, ozone, and aging. Silicone is a synthetic elastomer made from silicon–oxygen (Si–O) backbone chains, which gives it exceptional thermal stability, chemical inertness, and resistance to weathering, UV radiation, and extreme temperatures. Natural rubber generally provides better tensile strength and tear resistance, while silicone offers superior flexibility over a wide temperature range (from very low to high heat), better electrical insulation, and longer environmental durability. Silicone is less resistant to abrasion and has lower mechanical strength compared to natural rubber. Natural rubber is preferred for high-strength mechanical applications, while silicone is chosen for environments requiring heat resistance, stability, and long-term durability, which is why it is widely used in Silicone Uses .

sections.text: What Property Differences Exist Between Silicone and Latex? The property differences between Silicone and Latex are listed below. Temperature Range: Silicone maintains mechanical integrity from -60°C to 230°C, making it suitable for high-temperature and cryogenic applications. Natural rubber latex performs reliably from -50°C to 80°C, restricting its use in extreme thermal environments. Tensile Strength: Natural rubber latex achieves tensile strengths from 15 MPa to 30 MPa, significantly higher than silicone's typical range of 3 MPa to 10 MPa. The superior tensile strength of latex makes it preferred for thin-walled elastic products (gloves and condoms) where high elongation and tear resistance are required. Ozone Resistance: Silicone exhibits excellent ozone resistance across all service conditions. Natural rubber latex begins to crack at ozone concentrations as low as 0.01 ppm, requiring antiozonant additives in outdoor applications. Natural rubber accounts for 40% to 45% of the rubber compound in passenger car tires and up to 80% of the compound in heavy truck, bus, and aircraft tires, where high tensile strength and resistance to heat buildup under cyclic deformation are non-negotiable performance requirements. The low hysteresis of natural rubber reduces heat generation within the tire structure during high-speed rolling, directly lowering rolling resistance and improving fuel efficiency. In automotive components beyond tires, natural rubber is used in engine mounts, suspension bushings, brake hose liners, and door seals. Engine mounts made from natural rubber compounds with hardness from 40 Shore A to 70 Shore A isolate engine vibration in frequency ranges from 10 Hz to 200 Hz, reducing noise and mechanical stress transferred to the vehicle body structure. sections.heading: 2. Natural Rubber Used for Industrial Belts and Conveyor Systems
sections.text: 2. Natural Rubber Used for Industrial Belts and Conveyor Systems Industrial conveyor belts and power transmission belts are a major application of natural rubber, particularly in mining, quarrying, agriculture, and manufacturing operations. Natural rubber serves as the primary cover compound in heavy-duty conveyor belts, where the material's abrasion resistance, quantified by DIN 53516 abrasion loss values below 150 mm³ and tensile strength from 20 MPa to 28 MPa, withstands the mechanical demands of transporting abrasive materials (ore, rock, coal, and grain) over distances reaching several kilometers. Conveyor belt covers made from natural rubber compounds are classified under ISO 14890, with Grade M (abrasion-resistant) and Grade N (general service) designations corresponding to different natural rubber compound formulations. Natural rubber V-belts and flat belts used in power transmission applications exploit the material's high coefficient of friction (1.5 to 4.0) and fatigue resistance to transmit mechanical power efficiently. Operating temperatures for natural rubber conveyor belts are rated from -30°C to 70°C under continuous service.

sections.heading: 3. Natural Rubber Used for Seals, Gaskets, and O-Rings
sections.text: 3. Natural Rubber Used for Seals, Gaskets, and O-Rings Seals, gaskets, and O-rings manufactured from natural rubber are used in applications requiring reliable sealing of water, air, and non-petroleum fluids under mechanical compression. Natural rubber's compression set of less than 20% (ASTM D395) is the critical property that determines its sealing performance, as a low compression set indicates the material recovers close to its original thickness after sustained compression, maintaining contact stress at the sealing interface. Natural rubber O-rings are manufactured to AS568 and ISO 3601 dimensional standards, with hardness options from 40 Shore A to 80 Shore A and temperature ratings from −50°C to 80°C for continuous service. Gaskets for water distribution pipelines and industrial plumbing systems use natural rubber sheet compounds of 3 mm to 25 mm thickness. Natural rubber seals are not recommended for applications involving petroleum-based fluids, hydraulic oils, or aromatic solvents, where synthetic elastomers (nitrile rubber or EPDM) are the appropriate material selection due to superior chemical compatibility.

sections.heading: 4. Natural Rubber Used for Medical and Latex Products
sections.text: 4. Natural Rubber Used for Medical and Latex Products Medical and latex products represent one of the most technically demanding applications of natural rubber, requiring strict purity, dimensional consistency, and mechanical performance. Surgical gloves manufactured from natural rubber latex are produced through dip-coating processes, achieving wall thicknesses of 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm, tensile strengths above 18 MPa, and elongation at break above 650%, as specified by ASTM D3577. Examination gloves meet ASTM D3578 requirements, with a minimum tensile strength of 14 MPa and elongation at break of 650%. Natural rubber latex is used in the production of surgical drains, urinary catheters, Foley catheter balloons, and dental dams, where the combination of biocompatibility and mechanical integrity is required. Latex condoms manufactured from natural rubber comply with ISO 4074, requiring freedom from holes at a statistical acceptance quality level (AQL) of 0.065 at 100% electronic testing. Medical-grade latex products are processed using low-protein compounding to reduce Hev b protein content below 50 µg/g, minimizing the risk of Type I hypersensitivity reactions.

sections.heading: 5. Natural Rubber Used for Footwear and Shoe Soles
sections.text: 5. Natural Rubber Used for Footwear and Shoe Soles Footwear outsoles and shoe components represent a well-established application of natural rubber, where the material's abrasion resistance, high coefficient of friction, and flexibility at low temperatures provide performance advantages over synthetic alternatives. Natural rubber outsoles used in athletic footwear exhibit DIN 53516 abrasion loss values below 100 mm³, indicating high durability under repeated impact and abrasive contact with ground surfaces. The coefficient of friction of natural rubber on wet concrete ranges from 0.8 to 1.2, reducing slip risk in wet-condition footwear. Natural rubber is the preferred outsole material in high-performance trail running shoes, basketball shoes, and climbing shoes, where grip, flexibility, and durability are primary selection criteria. Rubber compound hardness for shoe outsoles typically ranges from 50 Shore A to 70 Shore A, balanced to provide grip without excessive stiffness. Natural rubber is also used in boot manufacturing for agricultural and industrial workers, providing waterproof protection with service ratings from −30°C to 60°C.

sections.heading: 6. Natural Rubber Used for Adhesives and Rubber Cement
sections.text: 6. Natural Rubber Used for Adhesives and Rubber Cement Natural rubber-based adhesives and rubber cement are contact adhesives that bond porous and non-porous surfaces through a combination of high initial tack and cohesive strength derived from the polyisoprene base polymer. Natural rubber adhesives are formulated by dissolving natural rubber (SMR or RSS grade) in hydrocarbon solvents, naphtha or hexane, at concentrations from 15% to 40% by weight, along with tackifying resins (rosin esters), antioxidants, and cross-linking agents. Peel strength of natural rubber contact adhesives ranges from 2 N/mm to 6 N/mm on standard substrates (aluminum and plywood) under ASTM D903 test conditions. Rubber cement, a solvent-based natural rubber adhesive used in bookbinding, paper crafts, and tire repair, achieves bond strengths sufficient for repositionable and permanent bonding applications. Rubber cement used in bicycle and automotive tire puncture repair kits bonds vulcanized natural rubber patches to tire inner tubes, with the solvent promoting surface diffusion and chemical integration of the adhesive with the rubber substrate.

sections.heading: 7. Natural Rubber Used for Vibration Dampers and Shock Mounts
sections.text: 7. Natural Rubber Used for Vibration Dampers and Shock Mounts Vibration dampers and shock mounts manufactured from natural rubber are used in automotive, industrial machinery, and civil engineering applications to isolate and attenuate mechanical vibration and impact energy. Natural rubber's low hysteresis, meaning minimal heat generation per deformation cycle, makes it the preferred material for vibration isolation elements operating under continuous dynamic loading at frequencies from 5 Hz to 500 Hz. Automotive engine mounts made from natural rubber compounds with hardness from 40 Shore A to 65 Shore A provide vibration attenuation of 20 dB to 40 dB in the frequency range relevant to engine and road-induced noise. Seismic isolation bearings, large-scale natural rubber shock mounts installed under buildings and bridges in earthquake-prone regions, use laminated natural rubber pads with steel plates to achieve lateral flexibility (horizontal stiffness from 0.5 kN/mm to 5 kN/mm) while maintaining vertical load capacity. Natural rubber seismic isolators are installed in structures (hospitals, bridges, and government buildings) in Japan, the United States, and New Zealand to reduce e...

sections.heading: 8. Natural Rubber Used for Rubber Bands and Elastic Products
sections.text: 8. Natural Rubber Used for Rubber Bands and Elastic Products Rubber bands and elastic products are among the most widely distributed consumer applications of natural rubber, relying on the material's high elongation at break and low permanent set after repeated cycling. Rubber bands are manufactured by extruding vulcanized natural rubber compound into flat strips, then cutting the strips into bands of specified widths (3 mm to 25 mm) and lengths (35 mm to 180 mm) per ASTM D5181 specifications. The elongation at break of rubber bands reaches 600% to 800%, and elastic recovery after stretching to 500% elongation and releasing is greater than 97% for high-quality natural rubber compounds. Elastic products (waistbands, bungee cords, elastic surgical tubing, and resistance bands) use natural rubber as the base elastomer due to its fatigue resistance over millions of flex cycles. Natural rubber elastic thread, used in textile elastic applications, has diameters from 0.3 mm to 2.5 mm and is rated for sustained elongation of 300% to 500% with full elastic recovery. sections.heading: What Are the Advantages of Using Natural Rubber?
sections.text: What Are the Advantages of Using Natural Rubber? The advantages of using Natural Rubber are listed below. High Tensile Strength Without Fillers: Natural rubber achieves tensile strengths up to 30 MPa in unfilled, gum compounds, a performance level not matched by most synthetic rubbers without the addition of carbon black or silica reinforcing fillers. The strain-induced crystallization mechanism of natural rubber's polyisoprene chains generates self-reinforcement under load. Superior Elongation at Break : The elongation at break of natural rubber reaches up to 800%, enabling the material to absorb large deformations without failure, a property applied in tire sidewalls, elastic products, and seismic isolation bearings. Low Hysteresis and Heat Buildup: Natural rubber generates less heat per deformation cycle than most synthetic rubbers, reducing internal temperature rise in dynamic applications and improving fatigue life in cyclic-loading components (tires and vibration isolators). Excellent Tear Resistance: Tear strength values from 30 kN/m to 100 kN/m place natural rubber among the highest-performing elastomers for resistance to crack propagation under mechanical stress. text_excerpt: Resources / Materials / Natural Rubber: Properties, Examples and Uses Natural Rubber: Properties, Examples and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 35 min read Published November 25, 2026 Natural rubber is an elastic, biodegradable material derived from the latex sap of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, known as the rubber tree, and is composed primarily of cis-1,4-polyisoprene, a naturally occurring polymer. Natural rubber forms through the collection and processing of latex, a milky white fluid that flows from incisions made in the bark of rubber trees, and the material is then coagulated, dried, and refined into usable sheets or blocks. Natural rubber originates from tropical regions, with Southeast Asia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Malaysia accounting for over 90% of global production. The material exhibits a distinct set of properties, including high tensile strength ranging from 15 MPa to 30 MPa, excellent elasticity with elongation at break reaching up to 800%, and strong resistance to abrasion, tear, and fatigue.
